matching.reasoningTemplate: Sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness and reduced breath sounds suggests pneumothorax.

clinicalPearls: Pneumothorax is simply gas within the pleural space; classify it as spontaneous (no preceding trauma) versus traumatic, and spontaneous further as primary (no underlying lung disease) versus secondary (underlying lung disease present) (Harrison 22e p.2313).
A tension pneumothorax is defined physiologically as one in which pleural pressure stays positive throughout the entire respiratory cycle (Harrison 22e p.2313).

Tension pneumothorax should be treated as a clinical emergency on the basis of bedside findings; do not wait for a confirmatory chest radiograph before relieving the pressure, because untreated tension leads to death from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2314).

When a tension pneumothorax is suspected, decompression precedes imaging: a large-bore needle is placed into the pleural space and a rush of escaping gas confirms the diagnosis (knowledge principle; no dose/technique detail) (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically results from rupture of small apical subpleural blebs (cystic spaces within or just beneath the visceral pleura) (Harrison 22e p.2313).
Classic primary spontaneous pneumothorax patient is a young, tall, thin man; smoking, male sex, family history, and Marfan syndrome are recognized risk factors (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105).
Symptom onset in primary spontaneous pneumothorax is usually sudden but dyspnea can be mild, so presentation to care is sometimes delayed (Harrison 22e p.104).

Tension pneumothorax most often arises during mechanical ventilation or resuscitation; difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or high peak inspiratory pressures on the ventilator should strongly raise suspicion (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Persistent air leak is a recognized entity, defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with an air leak lasting longer than about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2273).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pneumothorax is the accumulation of gas in the pleural space. In primary spontaneous pneumothorax, apical subpleural blebs rupture, allowing air to enter the pleural space without preceding trauma and in the absence of underlying lung disease. Secondary pneumothorax occurs when the same process complicates established lung disease, where loss of pulmonary reserve makes the event more dangerous. Traumatic pneumothorax results from penetrating or non-penetrating chest injury, and iatrogenic pneumothorax (a traumatic subtype) follows procedures such as transthoracic needle aspiration, thoracentesis, or central venous catheter insertion. In a tension pneumothorax, a one-way valve effect produces pleural pressure that remains positive across the whole respiratory cycle; this both severely compromises ventilation and transmits positive pressure to the mediastinum, reducing venous return to the heart and thereby cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314).
additionalDifferentials: Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.105)
Acute aortic syndrome / aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105)
Esophageal disorders such as reflux or motility disorder mimicking angina (Harrison 22e p.105)
Musculoskeletal chest-wall pain including costochondritis (Tietze syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.105)
infectionMimics: Pneumonia or pleuritis presenting with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea (Harrison 22e p.104)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary embolism, which like pneumothorax can cause sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and hemodynamic compromise (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105)
Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.105)
Aortic dissection / acute aortic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105)
Pericarditis with cardiac tamponade (Harrison 22e p.105, p.2293)
Esophageal reflux or spasm mimicking angina (Harrison 22e p.105)
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph to confirm or exclude pneumothorax; it is the routine first-line image in acute chest discomfort and is useful for pneumothorax, though for tension it must not delay decompression (Harrison 22e p.105, p.2272).
Point-of-care lung ultrasound (POCUS), which can rapidly diagnose pneumothorax (as well as pleural effusion and consolidation) at the bedside (Harrison 22e p.2272, shock evaluation chapter).

Bedside physical examination as a diagnostic tool for tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, mediastinal shift to the contralateral side, and hypotension (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Percussion to distinguish causes of diminished breath sounds: pneumothorax is hyper-resonant whereas pleural effusion is dull (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter).
Palpation for subcutaneous emphysema as a sign of associated barotrauma (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter).
redFlags: Tracheal/mediastinal shift to the contralateral side, absent breath sounds over an enlarged hemithorax, hyperresonant percussion, and hypotension — the bedside signs of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Hemodynamic collapse from trapped intrathoracic air defines tension pneumothorax as a medical emergency (Harrison 22e p.104).

Tension pneumothorax is a cause of obstructive shock and of pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest, and is a reversible cause to consider during resuscitation (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters).
Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mmHg) can accompany tension pneumothorax and signals significant hemodynamic compromise (Harrison 22e p.1813).
Tachycardia and hypotension in a patient with chest discomfort should trigger rapid evaluation for the most lethal causes, including tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.105).
Difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or rising peak inspiratory pressures on mechanical ventilation should prompt urgent suspicion of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314).
harrison.prognosis: Roughly half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax experience a recurrence. Secondary pneumothorax carries a worse outlook than pneumothorax in otherwise normal lungs because the underlying lung disease leaves little pulmonary reserve, making the event potentially more life-threatening. Untreated tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314).
pitfalls: Waiting for a chest radiograph to confirm a suspected tension pneumothorax instead of decompressing immediately — tension is a clinical diagnosis and delay can be fatal (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Underestimating a secondary pneumothorax in a patient with COPD, asthma, or cystic fibrosis; because of poor reserve it can be far more dangerous than a primary event (Harrison 22e p.104, p.2313).
Mild dyspnea in primary spontaneous pneumothorax can lead to delayed presentation, so a benign-seeming history does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.104).
Forgetting iatrogenic pneumothorax after thoracentesis, transthoracic needle aspiration, or central line placement (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Attributing absent or diminished breath sounds to effusion when percussion (hyper-resonant in pneumothorax, dull in effusion) would distinguish them (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter).
Overlooking tension pneumothorax as a reversible cause of PEA arrest and obstructive shock (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison classifies pneumothorax by mechanism and risk rather than a numeric score: (1) primary spontaneous (no underlying lung disease, often young tall thin smokers, frequently manageable conservatively if asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic); (2) secondary spontaneous (underlying lung disease present, e.g., COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis — more life-threatening because of limited reserve); (3) traumatic, including the increasingly common iatrogenic subtype; and (4) tension pneumothorax, defined by positive pleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle and treated as a medical emergency. Persistent air leak is a recognized complication defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with air leak beyond about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314, p.2273).
